claim: Did you know… the least skilled people are the most overconfident about their skills?

studies.finding: Random-number simulations showed that noise and a common graphing convention can produce the classic self-assessment pattern without any metacognitive deficit.
studies.verdict: Noise and regression to the mean can mimic the effect.

studies.finding: In 929 people, self-rated and measured intelligence related almost linearly, with no sign of the pattern the effect predicts.
studies.verdict: Effect likely much smaller than reported; a rebuttal and replication exist.

claim: Did you know… your startle reflex predicts whether you vote left or right?

studies.finding: In 46 adults, stronger physiological reactions to sudden noises and threatening images went with conservative positions on defense and social order.
studies.verdict: Small sample; widely cited for a decade without independent replication.

studies.cite: Bakker et al. (2020), Nature Human Behaviour
studies.finding: A preregistered direct replication and two conceptual replications found no stronger physiological threat response among conservatives.
studies.verdict: Failed in the US and the Netherlands.

claim: Did you know… washing your hands makes your moral judgments less harsh?

studies.finding: Participants primed with cleanliness, or who washed their hands after disgust, judged moral transgressions less severely.
studies.verdict: Original two-experiment report, small samples.

studies.finding: Direct replications of both experiments, with over 99% power, found effects near zero.
studies.verdict: Not replicated; the original authors dispute the analysis, citing ceiling effects.

claim: Did you know… holding a warm cup makes you see other people as warmer?

studies.finding: Briefly holding hot coffee rather than iced coffee led people to rate a stranger as having a warmer personality.
studies.verdict: Original two-experiment report.

studies.finding: Three high-powered replications of the study of warm packs and generosity, 861 participants in total, found no effect.
studies.verdict: No effect at any site; later replications also failed.

claim: Did you know… teaching to your learning style improves how much you learn?

studies.cite: Pashler et al. (2008), Psychological Science in the Public Interest
studies.finding: A review found abundant stated style preferences but almost no evidence that matching instruction to style improves learning outcomes.
studies.verdict: Required matching pattern not found; some studies contradict it.

claim: Did you know… speaking two languages gives you a lasting edge in executive control?

studies.cite: de Bruin, Treccani & Della Sala (2015), Psychological Science
studies.finding: Conference abstracts showing a bilingual advantage were far more likely to reach print than those showing none, indicating publication bias.
studies.verdict: Evidence is contested; funnel-plot asymmetry supports publication bias.

claim: Did you know… sleeping on a complex decision beats thinking it over?

studies.finding: For complex choices, people distracted with puzzles chose better than people who deliberated; deliberation won for simple choices.
studies.verdict: Original deliberation-without-attention report.

studies.cite: Nieuwenstein et al. (2015), Judgment and Decision Making
studies.finding: A meta-analysis and a 399-person replication found no unconscious thought advantage; positive results came from small samples.
studies.verdict: No reliable support for the effect.

claim: Did you know… a lucky golf ball makes you putt better?

studies.finding: Golfers told that their ball was lucky sank more putts than those given an ordinary ball.
studies.verdict: Original report, with a large effect (d = 0.83).

studies.finding: Two high-powered replications found the lucky-ball group performed barely better than controls, pooled d = 0.05.
studies.verdict: Not replicated; effect essentially zero.

claim: Did you know… a red shirt makes a woman look more attractive to men?

studies.cite: Elliot & Niesta (2008), Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
studies.finding: Across five experiments, men rated women as more attractive and sexually desirable when red was present.
studies.verdict: Original five-experiment report.

studies.finding: Three studies of 830 men, including a larger replication of a prior red effect, found no support for it.
studies.verdict: Failed to replicate; the literature remains contested.

claim: Did you know… online brain-training games make you smarter at everything else?

studies.finding: In a six-week online trial, participants improved on trained tasks, but the gains did not carry over to untrained cognitive tasks.
studies.verdict: Practice effects only, no transfer.

studies.cite: Simons et al. (2016), Psychological Science in the Public Interest
studies.finding: A review of the brain-training literature found improvement on practiced tasks but little evidence of broad or real-world benefits.
studies.verdict: Broad benefits unproven; some narrow claims remain open.

claim: Did you know… taking a test teaches you more than rereading the material?

studies.finding: Students who took recall tests remembered more after two days and a week than students who reread, despite feeling less confident.
studies.verdict: Original finding; rereading only won at five minutes.

studies.finding: A meta-analysis of testing versus restudy comparisons examined the size and causes of the testing effect.
studies.verdict: Effect has held up across the literature.

claim: Did you know… most radiologists searching for lung nodules missed a gorilla on the scan?

studies.finding: Observers counting basketball passes often failed to notice a person in a gorilla suit walking through the scene.
studies.verdict: Original inattentional blindness demonstration; widely reproduced since.

studies.finding: Of 24 radiologists checking scans for nodules, 83% missed a gorilla image much larger than a typical nodule.
studies.verdict: Held up in expert observers; most who missed it had looked at it.
